problem_domains.description: Discussion of quantum speedups and limitations for NP-hard optimization problems, including worst-case vs typical instances and approximation settings.
problem_domains.quote: Although it is widely believed that quantum computers will not offer exponential speedups forNP-hard problems, the story does not end there. As we have seen, most complexity-theoretic statements deal with worst-case settings for exact solutions. In practice, typical optimization problem instances could differ substantially from the worst-case, and thus, exponential quantum speedups in these more realistic settings are still possible in principle.
problem_domains.location: Page 11, Section III.D Takeaways from Complexity Theory in Quantum Optimization

problem_domains.problem: Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) and shortest path
problem_domains.description: Use of TSP and shortest path as examples of how problem structure and restrictions change complexity and solvability.
problem_domains.quote: A perfect example of this is TSP, which – in its most general decision version form – is bothAPX-hard andNP-hard. If we restrict to Euclidean TSP, where all points are in Rd and edge weights equal their Euclidean distances, then, remarkably, there exists an explicitPTAS to solve such TSP instances [61]. Shifting to heuristic algorithms for TSP, one can actually solve problems in practice with up to millions of variables. Lastly, if we were to consider the shortest path problem instead of TSP, where we just want the shortest path between two places, wewouldhaveaproblemin P.

problem_domains.quote:
Closely related to MDPs are optimal stopping prob-
lems. These problems are concerned with timing an ac-

computational complexity theory — highlighting where quantum advantage is possible in each
context. Then, the core building blocks for quantum optimization algorithms are outlined to
subsequently define prominent problem classes and identify key open questions that, if answered,
will advance the field.

solution_approaches.approach: Grover Search
solution_approaches.description: Use of Grover's algorithm as an exact quantum optimization method providing quadratic speedup for function minimization and combinatorial search.
solution_approaches.quote: The seminal Grover algorithm for searching an unstructured database achieves a quadratic advantage over classical search in terms of the number of queries to the database (i.e. the query complexity). In exact quantum optimization, this advantage translates to an advantage for function minimization [89] and can achieve a quadratic speedup over brute force search in many problems in combinatorial optimization [93].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA) / quantum annealing
solution_approaches.description: Adiabatic evolution from an easy mixing Hamiltonian to a problem Hamiltonian whose ground state encodes the optimal solution.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Adiabatic Algorithm (QAA) is another exact optimization algorithm, reminiscent of homotopy methods of numerical mathematics [97]. It assumes a problem HamiltonianH whose ground state corresponds to the solution of a corresponding optimization problem, as well as a so-called mixing HamiltonianHX.

solution_approaches.approach: Diabatic and counter-diabatic annealing
solution_approaches.description: Variants of quantum annealing that relax strict adiabaticity or add counter-diabatic terms to suppress excitations.
solution_approaches.quote: The practical implementation of the quantum annealing protocol often involves repeated finite-time runs [104] or, potentially, diabatic annealing [105]. This variant relaxes the constraint that the system must always remain in the instantaneous ground state ofH(t). Another variant is counter-diabatic annealing, where additional terms are included in the Hamiltonian to suppress the transition to excited states during the annealing [106, 107].

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE)
solution_approaches.description: Use of QPE to estimate eigenvalues/eigenvectors of Hamiltonians encoding optimization problems, potentially aiding ground state finding.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is an algorithm to estimate the eigenphases of unitary operators [111]. It allows the estimation of the eigenvalues of certain matrices and can be used to find the ground state and corresponding energy of various Hamiltonians [112–114].
solution_approaches.location: Page 12, Section III.C Quantum Phase Estimation

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum linear algebra toolbox (quantum signal processing, singular value transformation, block-encoding)
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum matrix algebra primitives to simulate Hamiltonians, prepare Gibbs states, and solve continuous optimization-related problems.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum signal processing [129] enables the simulation of sparse matrices, i.e., the implementation of the time evolution operatore−iHt for a matrix H and a timet, with optimal complexity. Phase estimation then allows to extract eigenvalues and eigenvectors of H. Quantum singular value transformation [130] generalizes this result in an optimal way and allows efficient simulation of matrix algebra such asA+ B, AB, and singular value transformationsP (A)... The block-encoding framework unifies input models for matrices... These tools find applications in preparing Gibbs states, matrix problems, and continuous optimization.

solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms (including variational and dissipative methods) to prepare or sample from Gibbs states for use in optimization and SDP/zero-sum game algorithms.
solution_approaches.quote: QuantumGibbssamplingplaysacrucialroleinvarious optimization algorithms, particularly in convex optimization as discussed in Sec. IVB1. Quantum speedups are possible because, under certain conditions, Gibbs states can be prepared more efficiently quantumly than classically.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Gibbs state preparation (thermofield double, VQA-based)
solution_approaches.description: Variational quantum algorithms to approximate finite-temperature Gibbs states using thermofield double states or truncated Taylor series free-energy objectives.
solution_approaches.quote: A variational method for quantum simulators to generate finite temperature Gibbs states through the preparation of thermofield double states was introduced in [142]... A different VQA approach for the preparation of Gibbs states suitable for NISQ devices was presented in [143] where the authors presented an algorithm in their paper by applying a truncated Taylor series to compute the free energy, and then selecting this truncated value as the loss function.

solution_approaches.approach: Dissipative Quantum Gibbs Sampling
solution_approaches.description: A dissipative algorithm using local update rules for Gibbs sampling, designed to be simpler and more feasible for near-term hardware.
solution_approaches.quote: Additionally, recent advancements in quantum Gibbs sampling, like the Dissipative Quantum Gibbs Sampling algorithm [134], offer a simpler and potentially more efficient alternative, as they utilize local update rules and are more feasible for near-term quantum hardware.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum SDP solvers (Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update, etc.)
solution_approaches.description: Quantum algorithms for semidefinite programming that leverage Gibbs states and block-encoding to potentially achieve speedups.
solution_approaches.quote: This method and its applications in algorithms like the Matrix Multiplicative Weights Update for solving general semidefinite optimization problems are further elaborated in [147–151]. Notably, these algorithms leverage Gibbs states for computing trace inner products.

solution_approaches.approach: Quantum-accelerated approximation algorithms via SDP relaxations
solution_approaches.description: Use of quantum subroutines to accelerate classical approximation algorithms such as Goemans-Williamson for MAXCUT.
solution_approaches.quote: Quantum Computing could be used to accelerate known classical approximation algorithms via Quantum subroutines. For instance, Semidefinite Programming (SDP) relaxations, as used in the famous Goemans-Williamson algorithm for MAXCUT [163, 164] or more general variants for QUBO [165], may profit from Quantum SDP solvers, cf. Sec. IVB1.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs)
solution_approaches.description: Hybrid quantum-classical schemes that optimize parameters of a quantum ansatz to minimize a cost function related to the optimization problem.
solution_approaches.quote: A family of randomized search algorithms, often termed as Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) [168], decomposes the original optimization problem into solving smaller-scale optimization problems classically and evaluating certain expectations quantumly.

solution_approaches.approach: Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE)
solution_approaches.description: A VQA to approximate ground states of Hamiltonians, used for QUBO/Ising optimization by minimizing the expectation of the problem Hamiltonian.
solution_approaches.quote: Originally proposed for quantum chemistry applications, the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) [186] denotes a class of heuristic VQAs to approximate ground states of Hamiltonians.

solution_approaches.description: A problem-inspired VQE variant using alternating problem and mixing unitaries to approximate solutions to QUBOs like MAXCUT.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [190] denotes a special case of VQE that can be applied to find good solutions to QUBOs.
solution_approaches.location: Page 16, Section IV.A.1 Unconstrained Discrete Optimization

solution_approaches.approach: Warm-started QAOA
solution_approaches.description: QAOA variants that initialize from classical approximate solutions to improve performance and inherit some guarantees.
solution_approaches.quote: Other variants adjust QAOA in order to warm-start it from solutions obtained by classical algorithms. The idea is to use a classical algorithm to compute an approximate solution, and then use it to warm-start QAOA to further improve upon the obtained solution [177, 178]. These approaches inherit some of the performance guarantees of the classical algorithms used for warm-starting and have been shown to significantly outperform standard QAOA on certain instances.

solution_approaches.description: QAOA-family ansätze that encode constraints into the mixer so that only feasible states are explored.
solution_approaches.quote: The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz, which shares the acronym QAOA, denotes a family of QAOA variants that encode constraints into the mixer such that they are preserved and the algorithm is restricted to feasible states.

solution_approaches.description: Use of QAOA iteratively to reduce problem size by fixing variables based on estimated correlations, then solving the reduced instance classically.
solution_approaches.quote: Another alternative approach to QAOA is Recursive QAOA [206], which uses the quantum computer to produce a sequence of reduced problems. Here, at each step QAOA is used to estimate correlations between variables, and the problem Hamiltonian is reduced by fixing the strongest one.

solution_approaches.quote: Another family of near-term compatible approximation algorithms for MAXCUT is given by Quantum Random Access Optimization (QRAO, also called Quantum Relaxation Algorithms) [215, 216]. solution_approaches.approach: Quantum Imaginary Time Evolution (QITE) and variational QITE
solution_approaches.description: Imaginary-time evolution to project onto ground states, implemented approximately via variational principles or Taylor expansions.
solution_approaches.quote: Another time evolution-based heuristic is quantum imaginary time evolution (QITE) [145, 218]... These include projecting the non-unitary evolution to unitary operations [145] or embedding it in a unitary of augmented dimension [220]. Another family of algorithms are VQAs that map the time evolution to an ansatz by means of variational principles [218, 221] or directly projecting a Taylor-expansion of the time-evolution operator onto the ansatz [222, 223].

solution_approaches.quote: A frequently used example is the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) [229, 230], where we do not average over the objective values corresponding to all samples obtained from measuring a quantum state. Instead, we sort them and only take the average over the bestα-fraction of samples... Another proposal is the Gibbs objective function [162]. The rationale is the same as for the CVaR, it puts more emphasize on good samples than on bad samples, i.e., it biases the expectation value.
